power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.formatted: After accounting for this case momentum, the onset of the 2022 floods was associated with an immediate, independent increase in malaria cases of approximately threefold (IRR 2.985, 95% CI 1.878-4.751, p < 0.001).
table.expanded: After accounting for this case momentum, the onset of the 2022 floods was associated with an immediate, independent increase in malaria cases of approximately threefold (IRR 2.985, 95% CI 1.878-4.751, p < 0.001).

None of the three interactions reached conventional statistical significance individually (temperature × rainfall: χ²(1) = 0.01, p = 0.92; post-flood × temperature: χ²(1) = 3.32, p = 0.068; post-flood × seasonality: χ²(2) = 5.40, p = 0.067), and none improved model fit by Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) by more than 1.4 points relative to the model without interactions.

None of the three interactions reached conventional statistical significance individually (temperature × rainfall: χ²(1) = 0.01, p = 0.92; post-flood × temperature: χ²(1) = 3.32, p = 0.068; post-flood × seasonality: χ²(2) = 5.40, p = 0.067), and none improved model fit by Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) by more than 1.4 points relative to the model without interactions.

None of the three interactions reached conventional statistical significance individually (temperature × rainfall: χ²(1) = 0.01, p = 0.92; post-flood × temperature: χ²(1) = 3.32, p = 0.068; post-flood × seasonality: χ²(2) = 5.40, p = 0.067), and none improved model fit by Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) by more than 1.4 points relative to the model without interactions.

A joint model including all three interaction terms simultaneously reached nominal significance on a combined likelihood ratio test (χ²(4) = 10.90, p = 0.028) and showed a marginally lower AIC (Δ = 2.9), but had a higher Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) than the model without interactions (Δ = 6.8), indicating that the added complexity was not justified once penalized for the number of parameters relative to the sample size (n = 83 months).

table.formatted: The log of the previous month's case count was strongly associated with the current month's cases (incidence rate ratio [IRR] 1.696, 95% CI 1.431-2.008, p < 0.001).
table.expanded: The log of the previous month's case count was strongly associated with the current month's cases (incidence rate ratio [IRR] 1.696, 95% CI 1.431-2.008, p < 0.001).

table.formatted: After accounting for this case momentum, the onset of the 2022 floods was associated with an immediate, independent increase in malaria cases of approximately threefold (IRR 2.985, 95% CI 1.878-4.751, p < 0.001).
table.expanded: After accounting for this case momentum, the onset of the 2022 floods was associated with an immediate, independent increase in malaria cases of approximately threefold (IRR 2.985, 95% CI 1.878-4.751, p < 0.001).

There was no evidence of an additional change in the underlying monthly trend following the flood beyond this level shift (time-since-flood term: IRR 0.990, 95% CI 0.979-1.001, p = 0.069), suggesting that the elevated post-flood case level has persisted rather than clearly resolving within the study period.
The pre-flood period itself showed no significant secular trend (IRR 1.002 per month, 95% CI 0.999-1.006, p = 0.23).

The post-flood trend showed a small, marginally significant decline of about 1% per month (IRR = 0.99, 95% CI: 0.979-1.001; p = 0.069), indicating the elevated post-flood level was largely sustained rather than rapidly decaying over the remaining study period.

table.formatted: Moreover, Log-transformed cases in the prior month were strongly predictive of current-month cases (IRR = 1.70, 95% CI: 1.43-2.01; p < 0.001), confirming meaningful month-to-month persistence in case counts beyond what seasonality and climate covariates alone explain (Fig <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">7</ref>).
table.expanded: Moreover, Log-transformed cases in the prior month were strongly predictive of current-month cases (IRR = 1.70, 95% CI: 1.43-2.01; p < 0.001), confirming meaningful month-to-month persistence in case counts beyond what seasonality and climate covariates alone explain (Fig 7).

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect.
